blocks.text: Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images of each other. Optical isomerism is commonly shown by octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands, for example the nickel(II) complex of 1,2-diaminoethane (NH2CH2CH2NH2), [Ni(en)3]2+. Its two forms are mirror images that cannot be superimposed; such a pair is called enantiomers.
Optical isomers rotate the plane of polarised light in opposite directions. The isomer that rotates it to the right is dextrorotatory (+); the one that rotates it to the left is laevorotatory (-).

blocks.alt: Two mirror-image forms of [Ni(en)3]2+ on either side of a dashed mirror line. In each, six N atoms surround Ni and each gives an arrow (dative bond) to Ni; the N atoms are joined in pairs by CH2-CH2 chains, one pair above, one at the side and one below, the side pair on the right in one form and on the left in the other.
